newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Seoul to send home rescued North Korean sailor.
newsitem.headline: Seoul to send home rescued North Korean sailor.

text.p: South Korea will send home a North Korean sailor rescued while drifting off a southern island, the Seoul Defence Ministry said on Saturday.

It is the first goodwill gesture by South Korea towards the North since relations between the two Koreas turned icy after a North Korean submarine landed 26 agents on a South Korean beach in September.

A Defence Ministry statement said the North Korean sailor, identified as Chung Kwang-son of the Stalinist state's navy, was picked up by a South Korean maritime police vessel and taken to the western port city of Inchon on Saturday.

"Our government plans to return the rescued North Korean soldier shortly through the Military Armistice Commission on humanitarian grounds and in accordance with his own free will," the statement said.
The commission overseas a truce signed in 1953 at the end of three-year Korean War.

Chung's boat drifted south from North Korea and was spotted on Friday about 21 miles southwest of South Korea's So Yonpyongdo island, which is close to the border with the communist North, South Korean police said.
Chung, 19, initially refused help from South Korean rescuers but later accepted a police offer, a police officer said.

"The North Korean man at one stage threatened to kill himself with an axe he was holding when he was asked to get on board our vessel but he later requested his rescue after repeated persuasion," he said.
The decision to send Chung back home came one day before South Korean President Kim Young-sam is due to meet U.S. President Bill Clinton to discuss the September submarine incursion by North Korea.
Clinton and Kim are attending the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum in the Philippines.
Seoul officials have said Kim will seek a tough U.S. stand against North Korea until Pyongyang apologised for the submarine incursion which has raised tensions on the Korean peninsula.
Of the 26 North Korean agents from the submarine, 24 were shot dead, one was captured alive and another is still at large.
The North insists the incident was an accident and demands the return of the bodies and the captured agent.
South Korea says it will resume assistance to the North only after Pyongyang guarantees it will not stage another incident such as the submarine intrusion.

Seoul recently delayed sending technicians to do site preparation for building nuclear reactors in the North, which were promised under a 1994 U.S.-North Korean deal that halted a suspected nuclear arms programme by Pyongyang.
Pyongyang has since threatened to end its nuclear freeze.
On Friday, South Korean Foreign Minister Yoo Chong-ha met U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher in Manila and agreed to preserve the 1994 nuclear agreement.
